claim: Expanded GGGGCC repeats in the first intron of the C9orf72 gene represent the most common cause of familial amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS).
source: Expanded GGGGCC repeats in the first intron of the C9orf72 gene represent the most common cause of familial amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS), but the mechanisms underlying repeat-induced disease remain incompletely resolved.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature establishing this genetic association.

claim: The mechanisms underlying repeat-induced disease in C9orf72 ALS remain incompletely resolved.
source: Expanded GGGGCC repeats in the first intron of the C9orf72 gene represent the most common cause of familial amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS), but the mechanisms underlying repeat-induced disease remain incompletely resolved.
evidence: This is a statement about the current state of scientific knowledge regarding C9orf72 ALS mechanisms.

claim: Zfp106 is a specific GGGGCC RNA repeat-binding protein.
source: Here, we identify the zinc finger protein Zfp106 as a specific GGGGCC RNA repeat-binding protein, and using affinity purification-mass spectrometry, we show that Zfp106 interacts with multiple other RNA binding proteins, including the ALS-associated factors TDP-43 and FUS.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from RNA pull-down assays and EMSA experiments shown in Figure 1.

claim: Zfp106 interacts with multiple other RNA binding proteins, including the ALS-associated factors TDP-43 and FUS.
source: Here, we identify the zinc finger protein Zfp106 as a specific GGGGCC RNA repeat-binding protein, and using affinity purification-mass spectrometry, we show that Zfp106 interacts with multiple other RNA binding proteins, including the ALS-associated factors TDP-43 and FUS.
evidence: This claim is supported by affinity purification-mass spectrometry data presented in Figure 3 and Supplementary file 1.

claim: Zfp106 knockout mice develop severe motor neuron degeneration.
source: We also show that Zfp106 knockout mice develop severe motor neuron degeneration, which can be suppressed by transgenic restoration of Zfp106 specifically in motor neurons.
evidence: This claim is supported by histological and immunohistochemical data showing motor neuron loss in knockout mice presented in Figure 2.

claim: Motor neuron degeneration in Zfp106 knockout mice can be suppressed by transgenic restoration of Zfp106 specifically in motor neurons.
source: We also show that Zfp106 knockout mice develop severe motor neuron degeneration, which can be suppressed by transgenic restoration of Zfp106 specifically in motor neurons.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from transgenic rescue experiments shown in Figure 2j-m.

claim: Zfp106 potently suppresses neurotoxicity in a Drosophila model of C9orf72 ALS.
source: Finally, we show that Zfp106 potently suppresses neurotoxicity in a Drosophila model of C9orf72 ALS.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from Drosophila experiments shown in Figure 4.

claim: The repeat expansion has been identified in more than 40% of familial ALS and in at least 7% of sporadic cases.
source: The repeat expansion has been identified in more than 40% of familial ALS and in at least 7% of sporadic cases (Majounie et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Majounie et al., 2012.

claim: One proposed gain-of-function mechanism is that toxic dipeptide repeat (DPR) proteins generated by repeat associated non-ATG (RAN) translation of the RNA repeats cause neurodegeneration.
source: One idea suggests that toxic dipeptide repeat (DPR) proteins generated by repeat associated non-ATG (RAN) translation of the RNA repeats cause neurodegeneration (Kwon et al., 2014; Mizielinska et al., 2014; Mori et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature (Kwon et al., 2014; Mizielinska et al., 2014; Mori et al., 2013).

claim: Another major proposed gain-of-function mechanism for C9orf72 ALS is via the formation of pathogenic repeat RNA aggregates that sequester one or more RNA binding proteins, leading to altered RNA processing and metabolism in motor neurons.
source: Another major proposed gain-of-function mechanism for C9orf72 ALS is via the formation of pathogenic repeat RNA aggregates that sequester one or more RNA binding proteins, leading to altered RNA processing and metabolism in motor neurons (Cooper-Knock et al., 2015; Haeusler et al., 2014; Lee et al., 2013; Prudencio et al., 2015; Sareen et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature (Cooper-Knock et al., 2015; Haeusler et al., 2014; Lee et al., 2013; Prudencio et al., 2015; Sareen et al., 2013).

claim: Zfp106 is a C2H2 zinc finger protein with four predicted zinc fingers and seven WD40 domains.
source: Zfp106 is a C2H2 zinc finger protein with four predicted zinc fingers and seven WD40 domains (Grasberger and Bell, 2005).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Grasberger and Bell, 2005.

claim: The mouse Zfp106 gene is located on chromosome 2 at 60.37 cM (Chr2:120,506,820–120,563,843 bp; Genome Reference Consortium, Mouse Build 38).
source: The mouse Zfp106 gene is located on chromosome 2 at 60.37 cM (Chr2:120,506,820–120,563,843 bp; Genome Reference Consortium, Mouse Build 38).
evidence: This claim is supported by reference to the Genome Reference Consortium database.

claim: The human ortholog, ZNF106, is located at human chromosome 15q15.1 (Chr15: 42,412,437–42,491,197; Genome Reference Consortium Human Build 38).
source: In addition, the human ortholog, ZNF106, is located at human chromosome 15q15.1 (Chr15: 42,412,437–42,491,197; Genome Reference Consortium Human Build 38), a region with strong linkage to a rare recessive familial form of ALS (Hentati et al., 1998), suggesting a possible role in human ALS.
evidence: This claim is supported by reference to the Genome Reference Consortium database.

claim: Human chromosome 15q15.1 is a region with strong linkage to a rare recessive familial form of ALS.
source: In addition, the human ortholog, ZNF106, is located at human chromosome 15q15.1 (Chr15: 42,412,437–42,491,197; Genome Reference Consortium Human Build 38), a region with strong linkage to a rare recessive familial form of ALS (Hentati et al., 1998), suggesting a possible role in human ALS.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Hentati et al., 1998.

claim: Mice lacking Zfp106 function show evidence of nondevelopmental neuromuscular degeneration.
source: Consistent with this notion, mice lacking Zfp106 function show evidence of nondevelopmental neuromuscular degeneration, also suggestive of a possible role for Zfp106 in ALS (Anderson et al., 2016; Joyce et al., 2016; van der Weyden et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature (Anderson et al., 2016; Joyce et al., 2016; van der Weyden et al., 2011).

claim: Endogenous Zfp106 was specifically pulled down by (GGGGCC)8 biotinylated RNA and not by the unrelated (AAAACC)8 biotinylated RNA oligonucleotide.
source: Endogenous Zfp106 was specifically pulled down by (GGGGCC)8 biotinylated RNA and not by the unrelated (AAAACC)8 biotinylated RNA oligonucleotide.
evidence: This claim is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 1a.

claim: Zfp106 directly binds (GGGGCC)4 RNA in vitro.
source: RNA EMSA performed with purified Zfp106 protein demonstrates that Zfp106 directly binds (GGGGCC)4 RNA in vitro.
evidence: This claim is supported by RNA EMSA data shown in Figure 1b.

claim: 30× molar excess of unlabeled self competitor, but not 30× r(AAAACC)4, competes with Zfp106 binding to r(GGGGCC)4, establishing specificity of the interaction.
source: 30× molar excess of unlabeled self competitor, but not 30× r(AAAACC)4, competes with Zfp106 binding to r(GGGGCC)4, establishing specificity of the interaction.
evidence: This claim is supported by RNA EMSA competition data shown in Figure 1b.

claim: Zfp106 binding to r(GGGGCC)4 was not competed by 30× molar excess of a mutated RNA probe of equal length.
source: Importantly, Zfp106 binding to r(GGGGCC)4 was not competed by 30× molar excess of a mutated RNA probe of equal length, nor was it competed by 30× molar excess of rCUG repeats comprising a MBNL1 binding site (Figure 1—figure supplement 1a).
evidence: This claim is supported by RNA EMSA competition data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1a.

claim: Zfp106 binding to r(GGGGCC)4 was not competed by 30× molar excess of rCUG repeats comprising a MBNL1 binding site.
source: Importantly, Zfp106 binding to r(GGGGCC)4 was not competed by 30× molar excess of a mutated RNA probe of equal length, nor was it competed by 30× molar excess of rCUG repeats comprising a MBNL1 binding site (Figure 1—figure supplement 1a).
evidence: This claim is supported by RNA EMSA competition data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1a.

claim: MBNL1 is an unrelated RNA-binding protein involved in myotonic dystrophy.
source: Likewise, MBNL1, an unrelated RNA-binding protein involved in myotonic dystrophy (Miller et al., 2000), bound efficiently and specifically to rCUG repeats under conditions in which Zfp106 showed no binding to the same rCUG sequence (Figure 1—figure supplement 1b) and, as previously described (Reddy et al., 2013), was not able to bind GGGGCC repeats (Figure 1—figure supplement 1a).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Miller et al., 2000.

claim: MBNL1 bound efficiently and specifically to rCUG repeats under conditions in which Zfp106 showed no binding to the same rCUG sequence.
source: Likewise, MBNL1, an unrelated RNA-binding protein involved in myotonic dystrophy (Miller et al., 2000), bound efficiently and specifically to rCUG repeats under conditions in which Zfp106 showed no binding to the same rCUG sequence (Figure 1—figure supplement 1b) and, as previously described (Reddy et al., 2013), was not able to bind GGGGCC repeats (Figure 1—figure supplement 1a).
evidence: This claim is supported by RNA EMSA data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1b.

claim: MBNL1 was not able to bind GGGGCC repeats.
source: Likewise, MBNL1, an unrelated RNA-binding protein involved in myotonic dystrophy (Miller et al., 2000), bound efficiently and specifically to rCUG repeats under conditions in which Zfp106 showed no binding to the same rCUG sequence (Figure 1—figure supplement 1b) and, as previously described (Reddy et al., 2013), was not able to bind GGGGCC repeats (Figure 1—figure supplement 1a).
evidence: This claim is supported by RNA EMSA data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1a and citation to Reddy et al., 2013.

claim: Zfp106 binds efficiently and specifically to GGGGCC RNA repeats.
source: Together, these data demonstrate that Zfp106 binds efficiently and specifically to GGGGCC RNA repeats.
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple RNA EMSA and competition experiments shown in Figure 1 and Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Patients with C9orf72 ALS show evidence of post-mortem nucleolar stress.
source: Patients with C9orf72 ALS show evidence of post-mortem nucleolar stress (Haeusler et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Haeusler et al., 2014.

claim: In cultured Neuro-2a neuronal cells, Zfp106 was primarily present in the nucleolus and in other discrete nuclear puncta.
source: Interestingly, in cultured Neuro-2a neuronal cells, Zfp106 was primarily present in the nucleolus and in other discrete nuclear puncta (Figure 1c).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 1c.

claim: In lower motor neurons from post-mortem human spinal cord samples, ZNF106 was primarily observed in the nucleolus.
source: Likewise, in lower motor neurons from post-mortem human spinal cord samples, ZNF106 was primarily observed in the nucleolus (Figure 1d,d′) and also showed occasional localization in other puncta in the nucleus outside of the nucleolus (Figure 1d′).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunohistochemical data shown in Figure 1d,d′.

claim: ZNF106 showed occasional localization in other puncta in the nucleus outside of the nucleolus in human motor neurons.
source: Likewise, in lower motor neurons from post-mortem human spinal cord samples, ZNF106 was primarily observed in the nucleolus (Figure 1d,d′) and also showed occasional localization in other puncta in the nucleus outside of the nucleolus (Figure 1d′).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunohistochemical data shown in Figure 1d′.

claim: Zfp106 is predominantly located in the nucleolus of C2C12 myoblast cells.
source: The localization of Zfp106 to the nucleolus is in accordance with previous studies showing that Zfp106 is predominantly located in the nucleolus of C2C12 myoblast cells (Grasberger and Bell, 2005), and taken together, the results presented in Figure 1 support a possible role for Zfp106 in the biology of C9orf72 neurodegeneration.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Grasberger and Bell, 2005.

claim: Abnormal skeletal morphology in Zfp106tm1a(KOMP)Wtsi homozygous mice was briefly reported as part of a large-scale phenotypic screen of genetically modified mice by the Sanger Mouse Genetics Project.
source: Abnormal skeletal morphology in Zfp106tm1a(KOMP)Wtsihomozygous mice was briefly reported as part of a large-scale phenotypic screen of genetically modified mice by the Sanger Mouse Genetics Project (van der Weyden et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to van der Weyden et al., 2011.

claim: More extensive phenotypic studies demonstrated progressive neuromuscular disease in the absence of Zfp106 gene function.
source: More recently, more extensive phenotypic studies demonstrated progressive neuromuscular disease in the absence of Zfp106 gene function (Anderson et al., 2016; Joyce et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Anderson et al., 2016 and Joyce et al., 2016.

claim: Loss of Zfp106 function caused a progressive neuromuscular phenotype.
source: Consistent with published studies, we found that loss of Zfp106 function caused a progressive neuromuscular phenotype.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2 and Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: Zfp106-null mice were born at normal Mendelian frequency.
source: Zfp106-null mice were born at normal Mendelian frequency and were indistinguishable from control mice until approximately 4 weeks of age, when 100% of knockout mice began to exhibit evidence of a wasting disease and loss of muscle strength (Figure 2—figure supplement 1; Video 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by observational data from breeding experiments.

claim: Zfp106-null mice were indistinguishable from control mice until approximately 4 weeks of age.
source: Zfp106-null mice were born at normal Mendelian frequency and were indistinguishable from control mice until approximately 4 weeks of age, when 100% of knockout mice began to exhibit evidence of a wasting disease and loss of muscle strength (Figure 2—figure supplement 1; Video 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by observational and phenotypic data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1 and Video 1.

claim: 100% of Zfp106 knockout mice began to exhibit evidence of a wasting disease and loss of muscle strength at approximately 4 weeks of age.
source: Zfp106-null mice were born at normal Mendelian frequency and were indistinguishable from control mice until approximately 4 weeks of age, when 100% of knockout mice began to exhibit evidence of a wasting disease and loss of muscle strength (Figure 2—figure supplement 1; Video 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by phenotypic data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1 and Video 1.

claim: Transverse sections of the quadriceps from 4-week-old Zfp106-null mice showed increased variation in fiber size and evidence of grouped atrophy with very few centrally located nuclei.
source: Transverse sections of the quadriceps from 4-week-old Zfp106-null mice showed increased variation in fiber size and evidence of grouped atrophy with very few centrally located nuclei (Figure 2a,b), consistent with neurogenic rather than myopathic disease (Baloh et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by histological data shown in Figure 2a,b.

claim: The histological findings in Zfp106-null mice are consistent with neurogenic rather than myopathic disease.
source: Transverse sections of the quadriceps from 4-week-old Zfp106-null mice showed increased variation in fiber size and evidence of grouped atrophy with very few centrally located nuclei (Figure 2a,b), consistent with neurogenic rather than myopathic disease (Baloh et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by histological data shown in Figure 2a,b and citation to Baloh et al., 2007.

claim: By three months of age, near end stage disease, Zfp106-null mice displayed extensive muscular atrophy and severe degeneration of muscle fibers.
source: By three months of age, near end stage disease, Zfp106-null mice displayed extensive muscular atrophy and severe degeneration of muscle fibers (Figure 2c,d).
evidence: This claim is supported by histological data shown in Figure 2c,d.

claim: The number of choline acetyltransferase (ChAT)-positive motor neurons was profoundly and significantly reduced in Zfp106 knockout spinal cords compared to littermate control mice.
source: The number of choline acetyltransferase (ChAT)-positive motor neurons was also profoundly and significantly reduced in Zfp106 knockout spinal cords compared to littermate control mice (Figure 2e–i), providing further evidence that loss of Zfp106 in mice causes a neurodegenerative phenotype.
evidence: This claim is supported by immunohistochemical quantification data shown in Figure 2e–i.

claim: Loss of Zfp106 in mice causes a neurodegenerative phenotype.
source: The number of choline acetyltransferase (ChAT)-positive motor neurons was also profoundly and significantly reduced in Zfp106 knockout spinal cords compared to littermate control mice (Figure 2e–i), providing further evidence that loss of Zfp106 in mice causes a neurodegenerative phenotype.
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple lines of experimental data including motor neuron counts, histology, and behavioral phenotypes shown in Figure 2.

claim: The CRISPR-generated mutation in Zfp106 resulted in an essentially identical wasting and histological phenotype to the KOMP allele.
source: Independently, we confirmed the knockout phenotype observed with the KOMP allele (van der Weyden et al., 2011) using CRISPR-mediated gene disruption by non-homologous end joining (NHEJ) and creation of a frameshift mutation leading to a premature stop codon. The CRISPR-generated mutation resulted in an essentially identical wasting and histological phenotype (data not shown).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from CRISPR knockout mice (data not shown in figures).

claim: Zfp106 is expressed in both skeletal muscle and motor neurons.
source: To gain insight into the cell autonomous requirements for Zfp106, we used the KOMP lacZ knock-in allele (van der Weyden et al., 2011) to examine Zfp106 expression using β-galactosidase activity as a sensitive method for detecting expression. This approach showed Zfp106 expression in both skeletal muscle and motor neurons (Figure 2—figure supplement 2a,b).
evidence: This claim is supported by β-galactosidase expression data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2a,b.

claim: There is a highly significant and dramatic reduction in Zfp106 expression in spinal cord of knockout mice.
source: We confirmed a highly significant and dramatic reduction in Zfp106 expression in spinal cord (Figure 2—figure supplement 3a).
evidence: This claim is supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3a.

claim: The ~80% reduction in Zfp106 expression is consistent with previous studies.
source: The ~80% reduction in Zfp106 expression is consistent with previous studies (Anderson et al., 2016; Joyce et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by RT-qPCR data and citations to Anderson et al., 2016 and Joyce et al., 2016.

claim: Restoration of Zfp106 specifically in motor neurons significantly suppressed the Zfp106 knockout wasting phenotype.
source: Importantly, restoration of Zfp106 specifically in motor neurons significantly suppressed the Zfp106 knockout wasting and muscle grip phenotypes and resulted in restoration of the number of ChAT-expressing motor neurons (Figure 2j–m; Figure 2—figure supplement 4), indicating a cell autonomous requirement for Zfp106 in motor neurons.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from transgenic rescue experiments shown in Figure 2j–m.

claim: Restoration of Zfp106 specifically in motor neurons significantly suppressed the Zfp106 knockout muscle grip phenotype.
source: Importantly, restoration of Zfp106 specifically in motor neurons significantly suppressed the Zfp106 knockout wasting and muscle grip phenotypes and resulted in restoration of the number of ChAT-expressing motor neurons (Figure 2j–m; Figure 2—figure supplement 4), indicating a cell autonomous requirement for Zfp106 in motor neurons.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from transgenic rescue experiments shown in Figure 2j–m.

claim: Restoration of Zfp106 specifically in motor neurons resulted in restoration of the number of ChAT-expressing motor neurons.
source: Importantly, restoration of Zfp106 specifically in motor neurons significantly suppressed the Zfp106 knockout wasting and muscle grip phenotypes and resulted in restoration of the number of ChAT-expressing motor neurons (Figure 2j–m; Figure 2—figure supplement 4), indicating a cell autonomous requirement for Zfp106 in motor neurons.
evidence: This claim is supported by immunohistochemical quantification data shown in Figure 2j–m and Figure 2—figure supplement 4.

claim: There is a cell autonomous requirement for Zfp106 in motor neurons.
source: Importantly, restoration of Zfp106 specifically in motor neurons significantly suppressed the Zfp106 knockout wasting and muscle grip phenotypes and resulted in restoration of the number of ChAT-expressing motor neurons (Figure 2j–m; Figure 2—figure supplement 4), indicating a cell autonomous requirement for Zfp106 in motor neurons.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the rescue experiments showing that motor neuron-specific expression of Zfp106 is sufficient to suppress the phenotype.

claim: Thirty-nine proteins specifically interacted with Zfp106 in mass spectrometry experiments.
source: These experiments identified thirty-nine proteins that specifically interacted with Zfp106 (Figure 3a; Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by affinity purification-mass spectrometry data shown in Figure 3a and Supplementary file 1.

claim: Gene ontology (GO) and protein complex analyses revealed a significant enrichment in interactors with roles in RNA processing, metabolism, and splicing.
source: Gene ontology (GO) and protein complex analyses revealed a significant enrichment in interactors with roles in RNA processing, metabolism, and splicing (Figure 3a,b; Supplementary file 2), suggesting that Zfp106 may also play roles in these processes.
evidence: This claim is supported by GO analysis data shown in Figure 3a,b and Supplementary file 2.

claim: Zfp106 may play roles in RNA processing, metabolism, and splicing.
source: Gene ontology (GO) and protein complex analyses revealed a significant enrichment in interactors with roles in RNA processing, metabolism, and splicing (Figure 3a,b; Supplementary file 2), suggesting that Zfp106 may also play roles in these processes.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the GO analysis of Zfp106-interacting proteins.

claim: There is growing and compelling genetic and pathological evidence that dysregulated RNA processing and metabolism contribute to the development of ALS and C9orf72 ALS in particular.
source: There is growing and compelling genetic and pathological evidence that dysregulated RNA processing and metabolism contribute to the development of ALS and C9orf72 ALS in particular (Ling et al., 2013; Prudencio et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Ling et al., 2013 and Prudencio et al., 2015.

claim: Several of the Zfp106-interacting proteins identified are proteins directly associated with ALS and/or C9orf72 ALS, including splicing factors TDP-43 and FUS, the nucleolar protein Nucleolin, and the nuclear pore component Nup107.
source: Interestingly, several of the Zfp106-interacting proteins identified in our affinity purification-mass spectrometry experiment are proteins directly associated with ALS and/or C9orf72 ALS, including splicing factors TDP-43 and FUS, the nucleolar protein Nucleolin, and the nuclear pore component Nup107 (Freibaum et al., 2015; Haeusler et al., 2014; Lagier-Tourenne et al., 2010; Ling et al., 2013); Figure 3c; Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by mass spectrometry data shown in Figure 3c and Supplementary file 1, and citations to published literature (Freibaum et al., 2015; Haeusler et al., 2014; Lagier-Tourenne et al., 2010; Ling et al., 2013).

claim: Endogenous TDP43 and Nup107 coimmunoprecipitated with Zfp106 in Neuro-2a cells.
source: We further examined the interaction of Zfp106 with TDP-43 and Nup107, as examples of interacting proteins, by anti-Flag-Zfp106 immunoprecipitation followed by western blot for TDP43 and Nup107 in Neuro-2a cells (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by coimmunoprecipitation and western blot data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: Zfp106 is part of an RNA metabolic pathway (or pathways) that when dysregulated leads to neurodegeneration.
source: These experiments confirmed and validated the interaction with these other ALS-associated proteins and support the notion that Zfp106 is part of an RNA metabolic pathway (or pathways) that when dysregulated leads to neurodegeneration.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the interaction data and the known roles of the interacting proteins in ALS.

claim: Expression of 30 tandem copies of the GGGGCC hexanucleotide in the 5′-untranslated region of a UAS-dependent gfp transcript (30R-GFP) in glutamatergic neurons using OK371-GAL4 caused ~50% lethality due to an apparent failure of flies to eclose from the pupal case.
source: Expression of 30 tandem copies of the GGGGCC hexanucleotide in the 5′-untranslated region of a UAS-dependent gfp transcript (30R-GFP) in glutamatergic neurons using OK371-GAL4 (Mahr and Aberle, 2006) caused ~50% lethality due to an apparent failure of flies to eclose from the pupal case (Figure 4a).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from Drosophila crosses shown in Figure 4a.

claim: 28 day-old OK371; 30R-GFP-expressing flies that did manage to successfully eclose exhibited profound defects in locomotor activity compared to control flies.
source: Furthermore, 28 day-old OK371; 30R-GFP-expressing flies that did manage to successfully eclose exhibited profound defects in locomotor activity compared to control flies (Figure 4b).
evidence: This claim is supported by RING assay data shown in Figure 4b.

claim: No overt eclosion or locomotor phenotype was observed in flies expressing GFP only, 3R-GFP, or Zfp106 alone in glutamatergic neurons.
source: No overt eclosion or locomotor phenotype was observed in flies expressing GFP only, 3R-GFP, or Zfp106 alone in glutamatergic neurons (Figure 4a,b).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from Drosophila crosses and RING assays shown in Figure 4a,b.

claim: Expression of 30R-GFP causes a reduction in the number of active zones in Drosophila larval neuromuscular junctions.
source: Previous studies have also shown that expression of 30R-GFP causes a reduction in the number of active zones in Drosophila larval neuromuscular junctions (Zhang et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Zhang et al., 2015.

claim: Expression of 30R-GFP reduced active zones as measured by anti-Bruchpilot (Brp) immunofluorescence and quantification.
source: Consistent with those studies, we found that expression of 30R-GFP reduced active zones as measured by anti-Bruchpilot (Brp) immunofluorescence and quantification (Figure 4c–f).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunofluorescence and quantification data shown in Figure 4c–f.

claim: Co-expression of Zfp106 with 30R-GFP restored Brp expression at larval active zones.
source: Remarkably, co-expression of Zfp106 with 30R-GFP restored Brp expression at larval active zones (Figure 4c–f) and completely suppressed the ~50% lethality caused by expression of 30R-GFP (Figure 4a).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunofluorescence and quantification data shown in Figure 4c–f.

claim: Co-expression of Zfp106 completely suppressed the ~50% lethality caused by expression of 30R-GFP.
source: Remarkably, co-expression of Zfp106 with 30R-GFP restored Brp expression at larval active zones (Figure 4c–f) and completely suppressed the ~50% lethality caused by expression of 30R-GFP (Figure 4a).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from Drosophila crosses shown in Figure 4a.

claim: Co-expression of Zfp106 partially suppressed the adult locomotor defect caused by expression of 30R-GFP.
source: Moreover, co-expression of Zfp106 partially suppressed the adult locomotor defect caused by expression of 30R-GFP (Figure 4b).
evidence: This claim is supported by RING assay data shown in Figure 4b.

claim: Co-expression of Zfp106 did not result in a reduction in the expression of 30R-GFP mRNA.
source: Importantly, co-expression of Zfp106 did not result in a reduction in the expression of 30R-GFP mRNA Figure 4—figure supplement 1b), indicating that the suppression of the neurotoxic phenotype in Drosophila was not due to dilution of GAL4 protein.
evidence: This claim is supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1b.

claim: The suppression of the neurotoxic phenotype in Drosophila was not due to dilution of GAL4 protein.
source: Importantly, co-expression of Zfp106 did not result in a reduction in the expression of 30R-GFP mRNA Figure 4—figure supplement 1b), indicating that the suppression of the neurotoxic phenotype in Drosophila was not due to dilution of GAL4 protein.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the RT-qPCR data showing no reduction in 30R-GFP mRNA levels.

claim: Zfp106 is a potent suppressor of neurodegeneration in a C9orf72 ALS model.
source: Taken together, these data show that Zfp106 is a potent suppressor of neurodegeneration in a C9orf72 ALS model, and the results from this gain-of-function model support the idea that Zfp106 functionally interacts with C9orf72 GGGGCC RNA repeats.
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple lines of experimental data from Drosophila experiments shown in Figure 4.

claim: Zfp106 functionally interacts with C9orf72 GGGGCC RNA repeats.
source: Taken together, these data show that Zfp106 is a potent suppressor of neurodegeneration in a C9orf72 ALS model, and the results from this gain-of-function model support the idea that Zfp106 functionally interacts with C9orf72 GGGGCC RNA repeats.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the combined results of binding studies and functional rescue experiments.

claim: The ability of Zfp106 to suppress the neurotoxic gain-of-function effect of rGGGGCC repeats has important implications for understanding and possibly ameliorating the pathology of C9orf72 ALS.
source: The ability of Zfp106 to suppress the neurotoxic gain-of-function effect of rGGGGCC repeats has important implications for understanding and possibly ameliorating the pathology of C9orf72 ALS.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about the potential implications of the findings.

claim: Previous studies have suggested roles for Zfp106 in rDNA transcription and in pre-rRNA processing.
source: Previous studies have suggested roles for Zfp106 in rDNA transcription and in pre-rRNA processing (Ide and Dejardin, 2015; Tafforeau et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Ide and Dejardin, 2015 and Tafforeau et al., 2013.

claim: Zfp106 was identified as a polyadenylated mRNA binding protein in an interactome capture study aimed at defining an atlas of mammalian mRNA binding proteins.
source: Zfp106 was also identified as a polyadenylated mRNA binding protein in an interactome capture study aimed at defining an atlas of mammalian mRNA binding proteins (Castello et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Castello et al., 2012.

claim: Sequestration of Zfp106 by the expanded repeats may disrupt normal Zfp106 function in patients with C9orf72 ALS in a sponge-like mechanism.
source: A simple model is that sequestration of Zfp106 by the expanded repeats disrupts normal Zfp106 function in patients with C9orf72 ALS in a sponge-like mechanism (Cooper-Knock et al., 2014; Mizielinska and Isaacs, 2014).
evidence: This is a speculative model proposed by the authors, supported by citations to Cooper-Knock et al., 2014 and Mizielinska and Isaacs, 2014.

claim: Zfp106 may play functions important in the biology of C9orf72, such as influencing dipeptide repeat protein (DPR) production or affecting nucleolar function or nucleocytoplasmic transport via interactions with Nucleolin or Nup107.
source: Alternatively, one might speculate that Zfp106 plays other functions important in the biology of C9orf72, such as influencing dipeptide repeat protein (DPR) production or affecting nucleolar function or nucleocytoplasmic transport via interactions with Nucleolin or Nup107, which have also been implicated in the pathobiology of C9orf72 ALS (Boeynaems et al., 2016; Freibaum et al., 2015; Haeusler et al., 2014; Jovičić et al., 2015; Kwon et al., 2014; Zhang et al., 2015).
evidence: This is a speculative statement about possible mechanisms, supported by citations to published literature (Boeynaems et al., 2016; Freibaum et al., 2015; Haeusler et al., 2014; Jovičić et al., 2015; Kwon et al., 2014; Zhang et al., 2015).

claim: Nucleolin and Nup107 have been implicated in the pathobiology of C9orf72 ALS.
source: Alternatively, one might speculate that Zfp106 plays other functions important in the biology of C9orf72, such as influencing dipeptide repeat protein (DPR) production or affecting nucleolar function or nucleocytoplasmic transport via interactions with Nucleolin or Nup107, which have also been implicated in the pathobiology of C9orf72 ALS (Boeynaems et al., 2016; Freibaum et al., 2015; Haeusler et al., 2014; Jovičić et al., 2015; Kwon et al., 2014; Zhang et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature (Boeynaems et al., 2016; Freibaum et al., 2015; Haeusler et al., 2014; Jovičić et al., 2015; Kwon et al., 2014; Zhang et al., 2015).

claim: Zfp106 knockout mice show approximately 47% loss of motor neurons at 8 weeks of age.
source: Quantification of ChAT-positive neurons in the lumbar spinal cord of wild type and Zfp106 knockout mice at 8 weeks of age shows a ~ 47% loss of motor neurons in Zfp106 knockout mice.
evidence: This claim is supported by quantification data shown in Figure 2i.

claim: Body weight of Zfp106 knockout mice was significantly reduced at 2 months of age compared to control.
source: Body weight of Zfp106 knockout mice was significantly reduced at 2 months of age compared to control and further reduced at 3 months of age.
evidence: This claim is supported by body weight data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1b.

claim: Body weight of Zfp106 knockout mice was further reduced at 3 months of age.
source: Body weight of Zfp106 knockout mice was significantly reduced at 2 months of age compared to control and further reduced at 3 months of age.
evidence: This claim is supported by body weight data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1b.

claim: Zfp106-null mice exhibit profound loss of grip strength.
source: Zfp106-null mice exhibit profound loss of grip strength; grip score: 1, 1–10 s; 2, 11–25 s; 3, 26–60 s; 4, 61–90 s; 5, > 90 s.
evidence: This claim is supported by grip strength data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1c.

claim: Expression of Zfp106 mRNA is drastically and significantly reduced in lumbar spinal cord of both KOMP and CRISPR knockout mice.
source: Expression of Zfp106 mRNA is drastically and significantly reduced in lumbar spinal cord of both KOMP and CRISPR knockout mice.
evidence: This claim is supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3a.

claim: Expression of Zfp106 mRNA ranged from ~1.5 to 2 fold of wild type expression in two independent transgenic mouse lines expressing HB9-Zfp106.
source: Expression of Zfp106 mRNA ranged from ~1.5 to 2 fold of wild type expression in two independent transgenic mouse lines, as assessed by qPCR with primers amplifying both endogenous and transgenic Zfp106.
evidence: This claim is supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3c.

claim: A two-way ANOVA analysis of the locomotor data revealed a significant effect of repeat expression (p<0.0001) and Zfp106 expression (p<0.01) on locomotor activity, with a significant interaction between the two factors (p<0.01).
source: A two-way ANOVA analysis of the locomotor data revealed a significant effect of repeat expression (p<0.0001) and Zfp106 expression (p<0.01) on locomotor activity, with a significant interaction between the two factors (p<0.01); i.e. Zfp106 coexpression significantly suppresses neurotoxicity induced by expression of 30R (p<0.01) by Bonferroni's posthoc Multiple Comparison Test.
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of RING assay data shown in Figure 4b.

claim: Zfp106 coexpression significantly suppresses neurotoxicity induced by expression of 30R (p<0.01) by Bonferroni's posthoc Multiple Comparison Test.
source: A two-way ANOVA analysis of the locomotor data revealed a significant effect of repeat expression (p<0.0001) and Zfp106 expression (p<0.01) on locomotor activity, with a significant interaction between the two factors (p<0.01); i.e. Zfp106 coexpression significantly suppresses neurotoxicity induced by expression of 30R (p<0.01) by Bonferroni's posthoc Multiple Comparison Test.
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of RING assay data shown in Figure 4b.

claim: Zfp106 significantly suppresses the reduction in active zones caused by expression of 30R.
source: Quantification of active zones as total voxel occupancy by Brp signal at each terminal shows that Zfp106 significantly suppresses the reduction in active zone caused by expression of 30R.
evidence: This claim is supported by quantification data shown in Figure 4f.

claim: UAS-3×FLAG-2×STREP-Zfp106 (UAS-Zfp106) transgenic flies express Zfp106 in a GAL4-dependent manner.
source: The band in lane 3 migrating below the 225 kD marker indicates that UAS-3×FLAG-2×STREP-Zfp106 (UAS-Zfp106) transgenic flies express Zfp106 in a GAL4-dependent manner.
evidence: This claim is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1a.

claim: Zfp106 coexpression does not cause alterations in 30R-gfp mRNA levels.
source: Zfp106 coexpression does not cause alterations in 30R-gfp mRNA levels.
evidence: This claim is supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1b.
